boot.tip.angling.heading: Angling
boot.tip.angling.body: Turn your hull 20 to 30° away from the shooter. Angled side plates gain effective thickness, and flat-on armour is the easiest to punch through.
boot.tip.weakspots.heading: Weak spots
boot.tip.weakspots.body: Aim for the lower front plate, the turret ring and the cupola. A tier-X glacis will bounce almost anything; the hatches next to it will not.
boot.tip.camouflage.heading: Camouflage
boot.tip.camouflage.body: Standing still in a bush drops your spotting range dramatically. Move, and every bonus you were sitting on disappears.
boot.tip.gunhandling.heading: Gun handling
boot.tip.gunhandling.body: Wait for the reticle to converge before firing. A shot taken on a wide circle is a shot given away.
boot.tip.hulldown.heading: Hull-down
boot.tip.hulldown.body: Park behind a ridge so only your turret shows. Most tanks carry their thickest armour there, and the hull the enemy wants to hit is simply not on screen.
boot.tip.tracks.heading: Tracks
boot.tip.tracks.body: A tracked vehicle cannot turn or run. De-track a heavy at close range and you own the next twelve seconds of the fight.
boot.tip.sniper.heading: Sniper mode
boot.tip.sniper.body: Hold RMB, or wheel in past the closest zoom, to enter the gunner sight. Scope in for the shot and back out to move.
boot.tip.gunhold.heading: Gun hold
boot.tip.gunhold.body: Hold Caps Lock to keep the turret and gun still while the sight moves freely. Guided missiles follow the sight. Release to let the gun catch up.
boot.tip.spotting.heading: Spotting
boot.tip.spotting.body: You only see what your crew sees. A target that vanishes was never killed. It stopped being spotted, and it is still aiming at you.
boot.tip.shelltypes.heading: Shell types
boot.tip.shelltypes.body: APCR flies flatter and penetrates more; HE never bounces but barely scratches thick plate. Carry both and pick per target.
boot.tip.terrain.heading: Terrain
boot.tip.terrain.body: Soft ground and steep climbs bleed speed. Read the ground before you commit, because the fastest route across a map is rarely the straightest.
boot.tip.ammorack.heading: Ammo rack
boot.tip.ammorack.body: Modules and crew take damage separately from your hit points. A "healthy" tank with a damaged gun and a dead gunner has already lost the trade.
boot.tip.flanking.heading: Flanking
boot.tip.flanking.body: Rear armour is the thinnest plate on every vehicle in the game. Getting behind a heavy is worth more than out-shooting it from the front.

credits.body1: I designed and built Claude of Tanks as an experiment in how far one person can take an original browser game with persistent agent collaboration. Claude and Codex were development tools, not co-authors.
credits.body2: The vehicles, simulation, combat systems, interface, performance work, testing, documentation, and production pipeline were built end to end in a sustained workflow of many Claude and Codex agents. Every selectable tank is original procedural model work by Kevin B. Liu.

settings.controls.note.part1: Click a chip, then press any key, mouse button or wheel notch to rebind; pad chips listen for a controller button. Tap Esc to cancel; hold Esc to bind Escape itself. Right-click a chip to clear it.
settings.controls.note.part2: Gun Hold (Free Aim) preserves the current turret and gun lay while the sight keeps moving. Controller: left stick drives, right stick aims, RB holds the gun, START opens this menu.
settings.aim.note: Hold-to-aim: hold RMB to zoom into sniper, release to return to your previous view (aim pitch is preserved both ways). Toggle-aim: tap RMB to enter or leave sniper. Gun hold: hold RMB to preserve the current turret and gun lay while freely moving the sight. Caps Lock is always the dedicated gun-hold action; Left Alt remains its secondary default. Release to let the gun catch up. Shift toggles sniper mode.
settings.aim.sniper.touch: Swipe sensitivity and smoothing apply directly to the battlefield aim pad. Sniper sensitivity stacks with each zoom step.
settings.aim.sniper.mouse: Sniper sensitivity stacks with the per-zoom reduction, so high zoom always aims finer. Type exact values in the number fields for precise tuning.

settings.camera.isometricNote: Angled overhead view that keeps your tank centered, widens at speed and lifts over obstacles. Move the mouse, swipe or use the right stick to aim; zoom changes the overhead distance. Use your aim/scope control for sniper view. Applies immediately in all battles.
settings.camera.title: Camera
settings.camera.note: By default the chase camera keeps your tank clear of the battle HUD. Changes apply at once; in battle the camera moves behind this menu. Vertical framing moves the sight with the picture, and the sight still marks where your shell goes.
settings.interface.hideBattleUiNote: Keep aiming, ammunition/reload readouts, range, zoom and scope vision controls. Hide other battle panels. F10 switches full/minimal HUD; Esc opens Settings. Touch controls remain usable; three fingers restore the full HUD.
settings.interface.title: Interface
settings.interface.armorNote: In sniper view, aimed enemy armor is shaded from red (blocked) through amber to green (high penetration chance). The calculation follows the selected shell, range, angle, ricochet rules, ERA, tracks, and spaced armor.
settings.interface.hitValues: Blocked-shot values on directional hit indicators
settings.interface.hitValueNote: Incoming HP damage and outcome words always appear beyond their direction arcs. Enable this to append the authoritative pre-mitigation value to blocked results.
settings.interface.debugNote: Debug telemetry folds FPS, latency, frame pacing, render load, resolution, simulation, world, shadow, network, and memory diagnostics into one 4 Hz dashboard. It loads only when enabled.

docs.mp.seatsLede: Two sides and a gallery. The room sets its team size; empty seats can fill with bots.
docs.mp.seatsAria: {side} seats a side and {spectators} spectator seats
docs.mp.fact.capacity: A room holds up to {players} players and {spectators} spectators.
docs.mp.fact.balance: New players join the smaller side; the room's creator can lock team switching.
docs.mp.fact.bots: Empty seats fill with bots unless the room turns that off.
docs.mp.fact.tanks: Everyone brings their own tank, camouflage and up to {equipment} equipment items; two players can pick the same tank.
docs.mp.fact.names: Names are up to {chars} characters; a name already taken gets a number.
docs.mp.modesLede: A room plays any battle mode; the Proving Ground stays solo.
docs.mp.coop: In {modes}, everyone deploys on one side, up to {players} players, against the waves.
docs.mp.step.pick: Pick your tank, camouflage and equipment, then press Ready.
docs.mp.step.ready: The room's creator starts the battle once every connected player is ready.
docs.mp.step.host: The creator's browser hosts the battle; on a local network, the helper does.
docs.mp.fact.seat: Drop out and your seat waits {minutes} minutes; open the link again to take it back.
docs.mp.fact.migrate: If the host's browser goes away, the room hands the battle to another player within {seconds} s and play goes on.
docs.mp.fact.admin: If the creator leaves, the room's settings pass to the longest-seated player after {seconds} s.
docs.mp.fact.idle: A room closes {hours} hours after its last message.
docs.mp.fact.chat: Room chat keeps the last {history} messages, up to {chars} characters each.
docs.mp.fairHost: The host decides every hit, reload and result; the others send only their controls.
docs.mp.fairSpotting: You receive only the enemies your team has spotted: a hidden tank's position never reaches your browser.
docs.audio.hitsLede: No interface sound tells you a shot hit: you hear it at the target, late by the distance, and about half a second later your gunner calls it.
docs.audio.call.nonpen: It hit but did not go through: aim for thinner armor.
docs.audio.call.ricochet: It glanced off an angled plate.
docs.audio.call.enemy_crit: It went in and broke a module.
docs.audio.call.enemy_ammo_rack: His ammunition is burning: he is about to blow.
docs.audio.call.enemy_engine_hit: His engine is hit: he slows down or catches fire.
docs.audio.call.enemy_immobilized: His track is off: he cannot move until he repairs it.
docs.audio.call.enemy_crew_hit: One of his crew is down.
docs.audio.warningsLede: When something happens to your tank, the crew says so before you see it.
docs.audio.call.were_hit: A shot went into your tank.
docs.audio.call.bounced_us: A shot hit you and did no harm.
docs.audio.call.fire: You are burning: put it out or keep losing hull.
docs.audio.call.ammo_rack: Your ammunition is damaged: the reload slows.
docs.audio.call.engine_damaged: Your engine is hit: less power, and it may catch fire.
docs.audio.call.track_gone: A track is off: you cannot move until it is fixed.
docs.audio.call.gun_damaged: Your main gun is damaged until it is repaired.
docs.audio.call.low_hp: Little hull is left: get to cover.
docs.audio.call.sixth_sense: An enemy has spotted you; the sixth-sense lamp lights too.
docs.audio.call.missile_incoming: A guided missile is on its way: move or break its line of sight.
docs.audio.radioLede: Each nation's crew speaks its own language: {languages} crews in all.
docs.audio.fact.oneAtATime: One call plays at a time; survival warnings cut in front.
docs.audio.fact.damagedRadio: A damaged radio narrows the voice, adds static and drops words.
docs.audio.fact.crewSetting: Settings › Sound › Crew voices: National crews follow each tank's nation, or pick one of the {languages} existing national crews for every tank; the choice is saved across battles and reloads.
docs.audio.gunfireLede: Every weapon fires one of {classes} report classes; the bigger the gun, the louder and longer its report.
docs.audio.fact.hills: A distant shot is seen before it is heard, and hills between you and it muffle it.
docs.audio.fact.mars: On Mars sound travels at {speed} m/s and arrives {db} dB quieter and thinner.
docs.audio.fact.moon: On the Moon almost nothing carries ({db} dB less): you hear your own tank through its hull.
docs.audio.fact.sight: In the sight your own gun sounds from inside the turret, and the world outside dulls.
docs.audio.fact.powertrain: Each hull carries its own powertrain's sound: gas turbines spool and whine, diesels shift and rumble.
docs.audio.fact.tracks: Tracks change with the ground and your speed: earth, hard surface, mud, sand, snow and water.
docs.audio.fact.drone: An enemy drone buzzes where it flies and rises in pitch as it closes.
docs.audio.settingsLede: Settings › Sound has six sliders and two alarms; changes apply at once.
docs.audio.made: Every sound is a recording made for Claude of Tanks with ElevenLabs before release; nothing is generated while you play.

docs.topic.build.label: How the game was built
docs.topic.build.title: A browser game built through verified loops
docs.topic.build.lede: Claude of Tanks grew from a direct Three.js prototype into a typed, tested game through short implementation rounds: isolate one problem, change the smallest owner, prove it in the browser, record the result, and land it on main.
docs.topic.build.s1.p1: The project is browser-native and built directly on Three.js rather than a general game engine. The simulation runs at a fixed 60 Hz, playable tanks use first-party procedural runtime geometry, and presentation pages stay isolated from the heavy game boot graph.
docs.topic.build.s1.p2: Those constraints shaped the architecture: deterministic rules can run in Node, the renderer adapts independently, and every public claim can point to code, a test, a capture, or a measured receipt.
docs.topic.build.s2.p1: Movement, ballistics, armor, damage, spotting, match state, and bot decisions live behind renderer-free contracts. Three.js turns the latest state into cameras, rigs, lighting, effects, audio, and UI without becoming the authority for a hit.
docs.topic.build.s2.p2: That boundary lets local battles and browser-hosted rooms share the same combat rules. It also lets lower-end visual settings reduce cost without changing gameplay.
docs.topic.build.s3.p1: Claude Code and Codex were used as development tools across bounded tasks. Broad or risky work moved into isolated Git worktrees; each lane named the files it owned, preserved unrelated changes, and exchanged exact commit hashes and evidence before integration.
docs.topic.build.s3.p2: The working rule was simple: main stays current, unfinished experiments stay isolated, and a branch is not proof. Only the integrated bytes count. Human direction set the target and acceptance bar; agents implemented, measured, reviewed, and documented against it.
docs.topic.build.s4.p1: A typical round starts with a reproducible baseline, then attribution. The smallest plausible fix is tested with focused self-tests, browser interaction, console inspection, screenshots, and performance probes. A result must survive a second run or a deliberately hostile case before it is accepted.
docs.topic.build.s4.p2: Visual work is judged from current pixels, not only numeric checks. Performance work records cold and warm conditions, device constraints, long tasks, frame gaps, GPU resources, and transition timings instead of reporting a single FPS number.
docs.topic.build.s5.p1: Repository-level AGENTS.md, indexed subsystem SKILL.md files, and one maintained architecture decision record preserve ownership, invariants, required commands, and recurring failure modes without burying contributors in completed migration notes.
docs.topic.build.s5.p2: When a manual process repeats, it becomes a script or a gate. That is why model screenshots, combat anatomy, vehicle icons, route probes, public metadata, and release checks are reproducible from the repository. Raw execution receipts stay in Git history or ignored QA artifacts.
docs.topic.build.s6.p1: A finished change is committed as one coherent unit, rebased on the latest origin/main, and rechecked after integration. The final push verifies that its parent is still the remote tip so concurrent work cannot silently overwrite a newer landing.
docs.topic.build.s6.p2: The public build then proves route isolation and strips non-distributable comparison material. This keeps the playable site, source tree, documentation, and main branch describing the same game.

docs.topic.models.label: Procedural model pipeline
docs.topic.models.title: From reference to playable machine
docs.topic.models.lede: Kevin B. Liu authored every playable tank as first-party procedural runtime geometry. References guide proportion and detail, but the shipped machine is rebuilt from code, connected to combat data, rendered into its own icon set, and released through measured and visual gates.
docs.topic.models.s7.p1: Each supported wheel samples terrain beneath its own station. The visual suspension settles to those contacts, the hull derives pitch and roll from support, and the track path is rebuilt around the moved wheels. Swedish siege suspension adds commanded hull attitude without breaking gun tracking.
docs.topic.models.s7.p2: Track animation follows traveled distance and side speed. Damage can detach a side, remove its running band, throw a persistent ribbon, and leave loose running-gear pieces.
docs.topic.models.s1.p1: A model round begins with source photographs, published dimensions, plan and side references, or a comparison mesh when its license permits authoring use. The source is an oracle for recognizable shape, not a playable asset and not an automatic truth when the reference itself is wrong.
docs.topic.models.s1.p2: Proportion comes first: hull length and width, turret station, roof height, gun length, wheel count, track course, and major armor masses must read correctly before small fittings are added.
docs.topic.models.s2.t: Build the visible machine from parts
docs.topic.models.s2.p1: Procedural builders assemble hull plates, turret shells, mantlets, barrels, running gear, optics, hatches, smoke launchers, baskets, antennas, armor kits, and stowage from reusable geometry and material vocabulary. Station-section measurements keep front, middle, and rear masses faithful instead of stretching one generic box.
docs.topic.models.s2.p2: Camouflage-aware structural parts and neutral mechanical parts use explicit roles. Comparison GLBs never become a hidden production fallback.
docs.topic.models.s3.p1: Hull, turret, gun mount, recoil group, muzzle, wheels, return rollers, sprockets, idlers, and linked tracks have explicit owners. Turret equipment must rotate with the turret and remain visibly seated; hull equipment must not follow it. The muzzle bore must be open and resolve from the actual barrel hierarchy.
docs.topic.models.s3.p2: Suspension samples terrain at each support station. Native running gear preserves the correct wheel count and track path while avoiding duplicated donor wheels, clipping shoes, or floating attachments.
docs.topic.models.s4.t: Author combat anatomy from the same shape
docs.topic.models.s4.p1: Armor plates, spaced layers, ERA, modules, ammunition, fuel, crew, and articulation anchors are calibrated to the checked vehicle frame. The game therefore uses the same authored shape for presentation, impact tracing, internal damage, and the technical side diagrams.
docs.topic.models.s4.p2: Structural cupolas can participate in hit geometry. Sights, machine guns, baskets, antennas, and loose equipment remain presentation fittings unless gameplay explicitly gives them a physical role.
docs.topic.models.s5.p1: The asset pipeline renders the current procedural rig into garage and gallery imagery, transparent silhouettes, armor diagrams, separate module and crew diagrams, tier treatments, and supporting presentation views. One deterministic angle capture now emits both portrait sizes through a shared framing policy, so a new tank cannot leave behind a hand-cropped or stale thumbnail.
docs.topic.models.s5.p2: Use `npm run tank:portraits -- --ids=<changed ids>` and `npm run tank:portraits:check -- --ids=<changed ids>` for portrait-only work. The complete release sequence remains `npm run tank:anatomy:update`, `npm run tank:anatomy:check`, then `npm run tank:release:check -- --ids=<changed ids> --gate`.
docs.topic.models.s6.p1: Automated gates check geometry fingerprints, dimensions, stations, floaters, track intersections, wheel quality, muzzle bores, materials, armor anatomy, markings, provenance, and deterministic asset freshness. Standard front, quarter, side, rear, top, close, and yaw views then expose defects a numeric score can miss.
docs.topic.models.s6.p2: A model graduates only when every required view clears the visual acceptance floor, attachments have physical load paths, winding and backfaces are healthy, and the clean integrated release check passes. The Tank Gallery is the live inspection surface for that final procedural rig.

docs.topic.ai.label: Bots and tactical AI
docs.topic.ai.title: One bot controller for every battlefield
docs.topic.ai.lede: Solo and authoritative multiplayer bots use the same renderer-free decision logic. They navigate a seeded battlefield graph, respect team and visibility rules, choose viable shots, use vehicle capabilities, and remain testable without a GPU.
docs.topic.ai.s1.p1: Bots consume the same team, visibility, range, health, and vehicle-state contracts used by authority. They do not read rendered objects or hidden client-only coordinates. Candidate targets are scored from current tactical state rather than selected by scene proximity alone.
docs.topic.ai.s1.p2: Difficulty changes reaction, aim quality, engagement distance, and decision pressure without granting information the bot should not have.
docs.topic.ai.s2.p1: One typed traversability grid is built per match from terrain mobility, world collision, openings, objectives, and vehicle capabilities. The planner supplies deterministic paths around blocked cells while local steering handles immediate alignment and avoidance.
docs.topic.ai.s2.p2: Route decisions can be reproduced in Node across every map, including heavy vehicles, tracked damage, steep slopes, and objective modes.
docs.topic.ai.s3.p1: The controller respects turret traverse, elevation and depression, bore obstruction, reloads, magazines, dispersion, shell velocity, penetration, and target motion. It aims for hittable armor and internal weak areas when the current weapon and angle make that shot credible.
docs.topic.ai.s3.p2: Autocannons, single-shot guns, autoloaders, and guided weapons share the same decision boundary but apply their own cadence and ammunition state.
docs.topic.ai.s4.p1: Friendly vehicles are rejected from valid shot paths, and the controller avoids firing through allies. Bots spread their attention, move to useful lanes, support objectives, and keep enough separation to avoid turning one friendly cluster into an obstacle.
docs.topic.ai.s4.p2: Enemy bots and allied bots use the same logic. Team assignment changes targets and objectives, not competence.
docs.topic.ai.s5.p1: Bots consider exposure, cover, damaged tracks, disabled modules, repair opportunities, ammo state, and nearby threats. They can disengage from a losing angle, recover movement, re-path after destruction, and continue contributing instead of waiting in open ground.
docs.topic.ai.s5.p2: Mode objectives layer onto these survival decisions so capture, defense, escort, and horde pressure do not require separate fake movement systems.
docs.topic.ai.s6.p1: Focused AI tests cover aim, friendly-fire rejection, routes, difficulty, deterministic decisions, and authoritative bot integration. Map-wide server tests run the controller without rendering, while browser battles verify that visible movement, firing, and effects match those decisions.
docs.topic.ai.s6.p2: Bot changes run `node src/game/ai.selftest.mjs`, `node src/sim/ai.aim.selftest.mjs`, `node src/sim/botRoutePlanner.selftest.mjs`, and `node server/authoritativeBots.selftest.mjs`.

docs.topic.simulation.label: Simulation and authority
docs.topic.simulation.title: Every hit has a path
docs.topic.simulation.lede: The battle simulation advances at 60 Hz. Movement, aim, ballistics, armor, damage, reloads, spotting, and match results are resolved from authoritative state, not from the rendered frame.
docs.topic.simulation.s7.p1: The room Worker coordinates discovery and signaling. It does not run the sixty-step battle simulation. The host browser runs the match authority and exchanges WebRTC data with peers. Guests send inputs; the host resolves movement, firing, reloads, collisions, damage, bots and results.
docs.topic.simulation.s7.p2: The local vehicle predicts movement and reconciles against acknowledged host state; remote vehicles interpolate snapshots. Nearby and recently engaged opponents refresh more often than distant visible actors. Combat events remain ordered independently of those interest tiers. Prediction improves responsiveness but cannot award a hit or change the authoritative result.
docs.topic.simulation.s8.p1: Guest snapshots contain only enemies the viewer is allowed to see. Filtering occurs before encoding, so hidden coordinates are not simply sent and concealed by the renderer. Team vision and spectator perspective also govern nameplates, minimaps and presentation.
docs.topic.simulation.s8.p2: A browser host is still a participating player’s machine and must hold the authoritative world. Peer hosting should not be described as having the same trust boundary as an independent dedicated server. The protocol checks input ordering and message shape; it cannot turn an untrusted host into trusted tournament infrastructure.
docs.topic.simulation.s9.p1: Height fields answer vehicle support, projectile collision, camera clearance, and prop placement. Surface class affects grip and presentation. Roads, slopes, ridges, water edges, and hull-down positions are composed around the intended armored routes.
docs.topic.simulation.s9.p2: Vehicle suspension samples the same ground surface used by movement and ballistic terrain queries.
docs.topic.simulation.s1.p1: The authoritative step uses meters, seconds, radians, and a fixed 1/60-second interval. Input is sampled into explicit vehicle controls before movement, combat, spotting, and result evaluation run in a stable order. Render rate can change without changing the number or order of simulation steps.
docs.topic.simulation.s1.p2: Frame-time spikes accumulate into bounded fixed steps. Authoritative randomness is seeded or injected. Wall-clock time and `Math.random()` are excluded from rules that affect a shot, reload, module state, or match result.
docs.topic.simulation.s6.p1: Node-runnable self-tests cover movement, combat, spotting, missile guidance, special actions, AI aim, and the complete authoritative match. Browser probes add bore parity, projectile travel, live impact effects, and HUD alignment.
docs.topic.simulation.s6.p2: Run `node src/sim/combat.selftest.mjs`, `node src/sim/authoritativeMatch.selftest.mjs`, and `npm test` after changing shared combat rules.

docs.topic.rendering.label: Rendering and performance
docs.topic.rendering.title: Rendering can adapt without changing the rules
docs.topic.rendering.lede: Three.js owns presentation only. Adaptive resolution, shadows, vegetation, post-processing, particles, and warmup can change with the device; the 60 Hz battle model remains unchanged.
docs.topic.rendering.s6.p1: The garage does not build a battlefield until concrete Battle intent. Public pages do not import the playable renderer, and garage boot does not eagerly import the complete simulation or fleet graph. Exact vehicle-family and world work is acquired only when the selected route needs it.
docs.topic.rendering.s6.p2: Cold-load probes disable caches and record network plus application work so a warm navigation cannot masquerade as first-visit performance.
docs.topic.rendering.s7.p1: Battle entry acquires the exact world and roster, uploads required textures, prepares effects, submits vehicle materials, warms shaders and post-processing, and establishes the first valid camera before reveal. Required work finishes before the countdown instead of surfacing as a black or frozen opening frame.
docs.topic.rendering.s7.p2: Progress reflects owned stages. Stale work is cancelled when intent changes, and a retryable lifecycle owns recovery rather than scattering timers through the composition root.
docs.topic.rendering.s1.p1: The render path updates camera, visible vehicle rigs, world detail, presentation effects, lighting, shadows, and post-processing from the latest interpolated state. Established hot loops reuse scratch objects and pools rather than allocating each frame.
docs.topic.rendering.s1.p2: Late transparent effects share depth information with the main scene. Muzzle light, tracer, sparks, smoke, dust, fire, and debris are admitted by distance and quality policy.
docs.topic.rendering.s2.p1: Biome lighting supplies sun direction, sky, fog, exposure, and shadow policy. Stable cascaded shadows follow the relevant camera region. The post chain combines ambient occlusion, anti-aliasing, bloom where useful, output grading, and the final dynamic render scale.
docs.topic.rendering.s2.p2: Capture views pin quality and render scale so comparison images do not drift. Gameplay can reduce expensive layers under sustained load.
docs.topic.rendering.s3.p1: Desktop and mobile resolve separate starting profiles. Internal resolution, shadow work, vegetation density, effect budgets, and post features can step down independently. Hysteresis prevents rapid oscillation.
docs.topic.rendering.s3.p2: Device diagnostics and measured overload, not user-agent labels alone, select the safe path. A quality change never alters shell travel, spotting, damage, or authoritative timing.
docs.topic.rendering.s5.p1: Performance traces record frame categories, renderer counters, dynamic scale, and transition budgets. Browser probes cover cold load, battle entry, map switching, the garage, and multiplayer rendering.
docs.topic.rendering.s5.p2: Use `npm run perf:dev`, `npm run perf:cold`, `npm run perf:transitions`, and a production build for renderer work.

docs.topic.filming.lede: The site's fifty takes, its portraits and its four films were shot in Scene Studio on the game's own maps, tanks and effects. Each take is code: staged by a search, judged as a schematic previz, reviewed in the engine, fixed at its source and rendered as a supersampled 4K final with its own sound.
docs.topic.filming.s1.p1: Every take on the site is a scene document, not a recording: the map, the time of day and the weather, the cast and its paint, each tank's route and speed, where each gun points, the camera's rail and the moment for its still. `tools/media-r5/site50.mjs` writes all fifty from one table, so a change to the plan reaches every take that shares it. The shot library keeps each take's scene exactly as the Studio saves it, so a take opens in the Studio from a link: the viewer below opens every featured take that way.
docs.topic.filming.s1.p2: Each round is directed with notes: the lens on a three-dimensional track that swings close and far, tanks fast in every direction, fronts and quarters rather than rears, and a list of tanks that each lead a take of their own. Every round renders into folders of its own, so earlier versions stay beside the code that made them.
docs.topic.filming.s2.p1: Round four is the first loop, before the motion note. Engine review 1 is the first motion plan rendered small in the engine, with everything it caught. Previz is round six's plan as a schematic camera, and engine review 2 is that plan in the engine after the fixes. Engine review 3 is round seven: the plan re-staged on the 2.0 maps, the scenes the 4K finals render from.
docs.topic.filming.s3.p1: Ten steps take a shot from a note to the website. The checks run before any GPU time is spent, and every fix lands in the engine, the tools or the plan, never in a single frame.
docs.topic.filming.s4.p1: The motion search staged all 50 site takes and all 166 fleet takes. For each take it tries road and open-ground routes, columns and fans of escorts, guns held on their own targets and lens moves by kind (a swoop, a lead reveal, an orbit that rises, a cable run, a weave, an overtake), and it scores every candidate for close-to-far range, climb, front angles, speed and flank swings. The winners are written to a tracked plan file.
docs.topic.filming.s4.p2: Previz draws each plan as a schematic camera's eye beside the map, with the lens's distance and height across the take. Choreography is judged here, in seconds per take, before a single frame is rendered.
docs.topic.filming.s5.t: The battlefield as the engine holds it
docs.topic.filming.s5.p1: A survey of each map in the running game dumps every collision record (its footprint, height, crush threshold and canopy) with a 4 m grid of ground heights and water. An offline model rebuilds the battlefield from that dump and answers with the engine's own collision code.
docs.topic.filming.s5.p2: Routes are checked against it in 50 ms steps: a hull may crush what a battle hull would crush, and anything else fails the route, as does a start inside a building or a slope too steep to climb. The lens check samples the camera every 100 ms and casts five sightlines to the hero (its centre, nose, tail and both flanks) through every record and canopy; low cover never blocks, and a prop counts only when it is large on screen against the tank.
docs.topic.filming.s6.p1: A spline camera rail keeps fast moves smooth through every key. Each tank drives its own route at speed with its gun stabilised on a target, and a travel frame lets the lens ride a swerving tank without swinging with it. The Plan view shows the take from above (every route, the camera's track and view, the lens's distance and height) and scrubs with the timeline.
docs.topic.filming.s6.p2: Tanks on the timeline now crush what they overrun, by the battle's own rule: a hull fells a fence, a wall or a tree when it runs over it faster than that object gives way. The crushes are planned from the routes before playback, fire live as the timeline plays and replay settled after a seek, so any frame shows the same wreckage. At night the Studio's camera holds a moonlit exposure, 1.25 stops under the map's, instead of adapting the dark back toward day.
docs.topic.filming.s7.p1: All fifty takes were rendered small in the game engine before any final. The first review caught three things the schematic could not: tanks driving through intact props in about half the takes, props in front of the lens in six, and eight night takes lit like day under a starry sky.
docs.topic.filming.s7.p2: Each fix went to its source: the Studio's crushes, the battlefield model and its lens check, and the night camera. The second review renders every take again at 960 pixels with a light probe on each. When the 2.0 maps changed the battlefields, the motion search re-staged the takes the new layouts broke, and a third review rendered all fifty on them before the finals start.
docs.topic.filming.s8.p1: Finals render at 3840 × 2160 and 30 frames per second, in deep focus: sharp from the lens to the horizon, with no depth-of-field blur in front of the tanks. Each frame is the average of 8 to 48 complete renders at sub-pixel offsets across a 60° shutter; fast motion adds renders until neighbouring ones are at most 1.5 pixels apart. The jittered average replaces the game's temporal anti-aliasing, bloom and the grade run once on the average, and a sharpening pass finishes the frame.
docs.topic.filming.s8.p2: Each take also renders two 4K stills at a 2 ms exposure: its key moment and a close portrait where the tank is largest on screen, each chosen with the whole tank in frame, centred, nothing in front of it and no burst of dust just before. About a hundred stills become posters, key art and social images; the films' ProRes masters are kept, and the site's formats are encoded from them.
docs.topic.filming.s9.p1: Nothing in the films' sound is synthesized. The battle effects are the game's own recordings, placed from each cut's edit list with the engine's resolvers (the gun's class, the engine family, the track set, the map's echo tail and its ambience), and the hero's crew calls its shots on the radio, in its own language, over the engine's intercom chain.
docs.topic.filming.s9.p2: The score is generated with Eleven Music from a composition plan written from the cut's cue sheet. Its hits (braams in the sheet's chords, a sub boom, risers, a reverse swell and taiko) are generated sound effects, several takes each; the best measured take is kept and placed on its downbeat. Each film is mastered to −14 LUFS.
docs.topic.filming.s10.p1: Four films are cut from the takes as HyperFrames compositions: a trailer, a 30-second cut, a 15-second vertical and the lineup. Their edit lists are generated from the takes, and the HTML compositions render frame-exact to video.
docs.topic.filming.s10.p2: The owner reviews every round on one board: each take's frames, previz, engine reviews and finals side by side, with the receipts of every change. Notes go back into the plan, the engine or the tools, and the next round renders beside the last.

docs.filming.take.s05.title: T-14 Armata past the barns
docs.filming.take.s05.story: In engine review 1 the lens ran low through a line of trees and past a sandbag wall and a parked car before it climbed over the village. Round six leads the Armata head-on down the road, then flies back and up as it bears down.
docs.filming.take.s22.title: Hetman II under a walking barrage
docs.filming.take.s22.story: Engine review 1 lit this night like day: stars over sunlit fields, then the lens behind trees. The Studio's night camera now exposes for the moon, and round six moves the lens with the assault.
docs.filming.take.s21.title: T-90SM wedge in the fields
docs.filming.take.s21.story: The first plan skimmed the lens along the road past concrete blocks and a dragon's tooth a few meters from the glass. Round six stages the wedge in open fields, its routes and lens cleared against every prop.
docs.filming.take.s47.title: T-90A Burlak in the burning yard
docs.filming.take.s47.story: Another night the first review lit like dusk. Every night take now renders with the moonlit night camera; round six leads the column through the rail yard, then flies back and high over it.
docs.filming.take.s04.title: T-90M Proryv column on the country road
docs.filming.take.s04.story: One of the first three takes re-staged by hand for the motion note: the lens dives from high over the column to a low pass beside the hull and climbs away.
docs.filming.take.s13.title: K2 Black Panther races the farm
docs.filming.take.s13.story: Golden hour on Frontier Basin. In engine review 1 a tree's canopy swept across the lens as it climbed; the lens check samples the rail every 100 ms, so a pass like that now fails before it renders.
docs.filming.take.s44.title: M1E3 Abrams at the oasis
docs.filming.take.s44.story: Sunset over Sunscar Oasis: the lens leads the column, then flies back and high over the battlefield with the minaret in silhouette.
docs.filming.take.s11.title: Challenger 1 in the rail yard
docs.filming.take.s11.story: A telegraph pole stood between the lens and the tank for the first seconds of engine review 1, one of six takes where a prop hid the hero. The lens check weighs each blocker by its size on screen against the tank's, so a distant pole passes and a near one fails.

fieldGuide.camo.overview: Paint helps concealment when its region matches the battlefield. Staying hidden also depends on movement, foliage and firing.
fieldGuide.camo.0.title: Match the terrain
fieldGuide.camo.0.body: Auto chooses a matching seasonal pattern. A compatible manual pattern adds 3.5 percentage points to your own camouflage before firing penalties. Factory restores the stock appearance; choosing a country collection alone does not grant the bonus.
fieldGuide.camo.1.title: Put foliage on the sightline
fieldGuide.camo.1.body: Bushes conceal a tank only when they cross the enemy’s sightline. Solid terrain and buildings can block that line entirely. A green paint job in the open is not a substitute for cover.
fieldGuide.camo.2.title: Concealment is not cover
fieldGuide.camo.2.body: A ridge or solid building blocks a sightline that actually intersects it. Foliage instead contributes concealment along that line; it does not stop shells. Firing reduces your camouflage and removes nearby foliage benefits within 15 m, while more distant foliage can still help. The marked lines illustrate these distinctions, not a live visibility test.
fieldGuide.maps.overview: Read a battlefield as routes, sightlines and protected positions, not just a backdrop.
fieldGuide.maps.0.title: Choose a route
fieldGuide.maps.0.body: Open lanes favor long sightlines. Buildings, rocks and ridges divide the map into shorter engagements. Pick a route that gives your vehicle room to turn and a covered retreat.
fieldGuide.maps.1.title: Work the ridge
fieldGuide.maps.1.body: A ridge can hide your hull while you expose the gun. Your gun’s depression limit determines whether you can aim downhill without driving farther over the crest.
fieldGuide.maps.2.title: Cross exposed ground
fieldGuide.maps.2.body: The village crossroads joins several firing lanes. Check the exits before crossing, use buildings to break sightlines, and avoid stopping in the intersection. Terrain, slopes and water change traction; a route that looks short may still be slow.
fieldGuide.dossier.overview: Use the dossier to connect a vehicle’s numbers with its battlefield role.
fieldGuide.dossier.0.title: Compare like with like
fieldGuide.dossier.0.body: Start with role and tier, then compare mobility, protection and firepower. A high summary rating is a comparison aid, not a promise that the vehicle wins every duel.
fieldGuide.dossier.1.title: Read the actual values
fieldGuide.dossier.1.body: Check gun limits, ammunition, reload behavior and nominal armor. Garage bars compare peers; equipped bonuses appear alongside stock values so you can see what your loadout changes.
fieldGuide.dossier.2.title: Inspect the layout
fieldGuide.dossier.2.body: Open the Gallery’s armor, module and crew layers to see where combat volumes sit. These diagrams describe the game’s authored combat model, not real-world engineering measurements.
fieldGuide.performance.overview: Speed, turning, vision and survivability describe different strengths. Build a plan around the combination.
fieldGuide.performance.0.title: Acceleration matters
fieldGuide.performance.0.body: Top speed is a limit, not a speed you reach instantly. Vehicle power, ground resistance and slope affect how quickly you move between positions.
fieldGuide.performance.1.title: Keep a way out
fieldGuide.performance.1.body: Turning and reverse speed matter when withdrawing behind cover. Avoid exposing your side just to turn around after taking a shot.
fieldGuide.performance.2.title: Read visibility separately
fieldGuide.performance.2.body: View range helps you detect enemies; camouflage makes your own vehicle harder to detect. Neither ignores solid cover. Equipment-adjusted values describe your selected loadout.
fieldGuide.protection.overview: A hit is resolved against the plate it strikes. Nominal thickness is only the starting point.
fieldGuide.protection.0.title: Find the impact plate
fieldGuide.protection.0.body: Hull and turret fronts, sides and rears have different protection. A frontal armor number does not apply to the whole silhouette. Use the armor layer to inspect the actual layout.
fieldGuide.protection.1.title: Consider the angle
fieldGuide.protection.1.body: An oblique shot travels through a longer path of armor. Shell normalization, ricochet and overmatch rules also matter, so an angle alone cannot predict the result.
fieldGuide.protection.2.title: Protect weak areas
fieldGuide.protection.2.body: Angle with care: turning too far may expose a thinner side plate. Use terrain to hide vulnerable areas and recheck which plate the enemy can actually hit.
fieldGuide.ammunition.overview: Pick a shell for the target and the shot you can actually make. Penetration and damage answer different questions.
fieldGuide.ammunition.0.title: Compare penetration
fieldGuide.ammunition.0.body: The ammunition card shows penetration at close range and at 1 km where applicable. Compare the selected shell with the plate and angle you expect to hit, not just the enemy’s vehicle name.
fieldGuide.ammunition.1.title: Understand the impact
fieldGuide.ammunition.1.body: AP-family, shaped-charge and explosive rounds resolve impacts differently. Damage is not guaranteed by the listed penetration value; a bounce, failed penetration or external hit can produce a different result.
fieldGuide.ammunition.2.title: Watch the firing cycle
fieldGuide.ammunition.2.body: A ready round, a magazine reload and a missile channel are different states. Follow the active weapon’s readiness indicator rather than assuming every ammunition choice shares one reload.
fieldGuide.armament.overview: Hull direction, turret rotation and gun elevation are separate parts of aiming.
fieldGuide.armament.0.title: Turn the turret
fieldGuide.armament.0.body: The turret follows the aim direction within the vehicle’s traversal limits. A target outside the current gun direction cannot be hit just because the camera can see it.
fieldGuide.armament.1.title: Use depression
fieldGuide.armament.1.body: The barrel has a minimum and maximum vertical angle. At a crest, insufficient depression can leave the gun above a nearby target even when the target is visible.
fieldGuide.armament.2.title: Move the hull
fieldGuide.armament.2.body: Reposition the tank when terrain or articulation limits block the shot. In the Gallery, change hull, turret and gun controls independently to understand the available firing arc.
fieldGuide.modules.overview: An impact can damage a system inside the tank as well as reduce vehicle health.
fieldGuide.modules.0.title: Follow the hit path
fieldGuide.modules.0.body: Internal damage depends on which modeled volumes the damaging path reaches. The module layer shows their locations; a visible equipment detail is not automatically a damageable module.
fieldGuide.modules.1.title: Notice the consequence
fieldGuide.modules.1.body: Engine, tracks, gun and ammunition storage serve different functions. Read the damaged-system indicator to understand why movement or firing behavior has changed.
fieldGuide.modules.2.title: Protect the layout
fieldGuide.modules.2.body: Avoid repeatedly exposing the same vulnerable side. Inspect the selected vehicle’s actual module diagram rather than assuming every tank places its engine and ammunition in the same location.
fieldGuide.crew.overview: Crew stations are modeled separately from the mechanical modules they operate.
fieldGuide.crew.0.title: Locate the stations
fieldGuide.crew.0.body: This in-game X-ray shows the Abrams commander and gunner inside the turret. The colored figures mark internal stations, not passengers sitting on the roof. Open the selected-vehicle diagrams below for your tank’s own arrangement.
fieldGuide.crew.1.title: Read the role
fieldGuide.crew.1.body: The blue driver station sits forward in this Abrams hull. Driver, gunner, loader and commander have different jobs; turret stations rotate with the turret while hull stations stay with the hull.
fieldGuide.crew.2.title: Respond to casualties
fieldGuide.crew.2.body: The pink loader illustrates a separate crew station; vehicles with other loading systems may have a different crew. Injuries and mechanical damage are separate states. Check the affected role and available consumables before deciding whether to withdraw.
fieldGuide.equipment.overview: Three equipment slots tune a vehicle for your preferred role.
fieldGuide.equipment.0.title: Tune the weapon
fieldGuide.equipment.0.body: Use your three equipment slots to support a role. Weapon equipment can change reload, aiming or dispersion where eligible. These are gameplay modifiers; fitting an item does not necessarily add visible hardware to the model.
fieldGuide.equipment.1.title: Match the vehicle
fieldGuide.equipment.1.body: Mobility equipment helps a vehicle reach and leave positions. Availability depends on class and weapon system, and the loadout is saved per vehicle. Choose from the items offered for your selected tank.
fieldGuide.equipment.2.title: Read the improved values
fieldGuide.equipment.2.body: The stats already show your equipment-adjusted values, including rotation, dispersion and observation where affected. Conditional equipment still needs its activation conditions; stationary observation and concealment bonuses are not always active.
fieldGuide.special.overview: Use the fitted vehicle controls independently of the main gun. The labels below show default keyboard bindings; the live HUD reflects your own bindings.
fieldGuide.special.0.title: Launch smoke
fieldGuide.special.0.body: On equipped vehicles, the Smoke control launches the turret-mounted canisters. The default key is G. Open the Smoke entry for the real launch arcs, screen behavior and charge limits.
fieldGuide.special.1.title: Use the roof gun
fieldGuide.special.1.body: The default B key toggles a supported automatic roof weapon. It needs a spotted opponent, a clear firing lane and a target within its aiming limits and range. It is independent of the main gun; not every visible machine gun is an automatic system.
fieldGuide.special.2.title: Lights and special actions
fieldGuide.special.2.body: N toggles the fitted lights by default. Other controls appear only when applicable: ATGM selection, suspension and Gravity Mode jump each follow their own rules. Use the live control strip for remapped keys, touch controls, charges and cooldowns.
fieldGuide.layers.overview: Each inspection layer answers a different question about the same vehicle.
fieldGuide.layers.0.title: Appearance and armor
fieldGuide.layers.0.body: Appearance shows the rendered vehicle. Armor shows authored protection plates. A decorative mesh and a combat plate are different things; use the appropriate layer for your question.
fieldGuide.layers.1.title: Modules and crew
fieldGuide.layers.1.body: Internal overlays reveal system and crew volumes. Rotate the vehicle and turret to understand their placement and ownership rather than judging depth from one side view.
fieldGuide.layers.2.title: Surface markup
fieldGuide.layers.2.body: Markup selects visible surfaces for review. It records annotations and screenshots without changing vehicle balance, armor thickness or the playable model.
fieldGuide.markup.overview: Mark the exact surface you mean, then export enough context for another person to find it.
fieldGuide.markup.0.title: Pick a surface
fieldGuide.markup.0.body: Choose face or patch scope before selecting the visible mesh. The selection follows its owning hull or turret as you change the pose.
fieldGuide.markup.1.title: Add context
fieldGuide.markup.1.body: Use the inspection readout and annotations to explain the issue. Keep the camera close enough to identify the surface, with enough surrounding geometry to show its location.
fieldGuide.markup.2.title: Export the review
fieldGuide.markup.2.body: Save the JSON and PNG together when sharing a review. The JSON preserves the selection record; the image shows what you were looking at. Neither edits the playable tank.
fieldGuide.camera.overview: Position and framing are separate choices. Set the view to explain the subject before capturing it.
fieldGuide.camera.0.title: Choose the viewpoint
fieldGuide.camera.0.body: A side view explains length and gun placement; a top view explains layout; a three-quarter view shows overall form. Choose the angle that answers the question.
fieldGuide.camera.1.title: Frame the subject
fieldGuide.camera.1.body: Keep the important parts inside the frame, including a long barrel or the direction of motion. Moving the camera and changing field of view produce different perspective relationships.
fieldGuide.camera.2.title: Keep a repeatable view
fieldGuide.camera.2.body: Use Gallery view presets for consistent inspection. In Studio, save the camera transform in a shot or recipe so the same composition can be restored later.
fieldGuide.environment.overview: Set the battlefield first: its seed, lighting and weather establish the scene your actors will occupy.
fieldGuide.environment.0.title: Choose the world
fieldGuide.environment.0.body: Select a battlefield and seed before placing actors. A saved recipe keeps this context together so later work starts from the same intended scene.
fieldGuide.environment.1.title: Set the light
fieldGuide.environment.1.body: Day, sunset and night change the lighting mood. Check silhouettes and important surfaces after changing time of day; a pose readable at noon may disappear in shadow.
fieldGuide.environment.2.title: Review the background
fieldGuide.environment.2.body: Weather, terrain and surrounding objects should support the subject. Check the final camera view before adding effects, then keep the environment in the exported recipe.
fieldGuide.actors.overview: Studio actors are staged vehicles. Give each one a clear position, pose and purpose in the shot.
fieldGuide.actors.0.title: Add a vehicle
fieldGuide.actors.0.body: Choose a first-party vehicle from the roster. Each added actor is a separate instance, so two copies of the same model can occupy different positions and play different roles.
fieldGuide.actors.1.title: Stage the pose
fieldGuide.actors.1.body: Select the actor before changing position, hull direction, turret direction or gun elevation. These controls act on different parts of the rig; check the gun’s direction in the camera view.
fieldGuide.actors.2.title: Keep identity clear
fieldGuide.actors.2.body: Paint and staged damage help tell the story. When building motion or effect tracks, verify which actor is selected so a shot or movement is attached to the intended vehicle.
fieldGuide.effects.overview: Effects are timed events. Place the cause and the result on the same scene clock.
fieldGuide.effects.0.title: Choose the source
fieldGuide.effects.0.body: Attach a firing event to the intended actor, or place an impact at the intended terrain location. A beautiful explosion in the wrong place makes the sequence harder to understand.
fieldGuide.effects.1.title: Set the timing
fieldGuide.effects.1.body: Place firing, impact and destruction events at their intended times. Scrub around the event to check the relationship between the muzzle, target and camera.
fieldGuide.effects.2.title: Check the final frame
fieldGuide.effects.2.body: Smoke and debris can obscure the subject. Review the actual capture time and camera, then save the recipe so actor poses and event times stay together.
fieldGuide.timeline.overview: Camera keys, actor tracks and effects share one timeline. Their timing creates the sequence.
fieldGuide.timeline.0.title: Place key moments
fieldGuide.timeline.0.body: Set the opening composition, the action and the ending. Camera keys store viewpoints; actor tracks store vehicle motion. They are separate tracks on the same clock.
fieldGuide.timeline.1.title: Choose the transition
fieldGuide.timeline.1.body: A cut holds the previous view until the next key. Interpolated transitions travel between keys. Inspect the path between keyframes, not only the endpoints.
fieldGuide.timeline.2.title: Scrub and replay
fieldGuide.timeline.2.body: Move the playhead through the whole shot to check actor motion and event timing. A still frame freezes one moment; a video also reveals awkward transitions and late effects.
fieldGuide.output.overview: A capture is the image or video. A recipe is the scene data needed to rebuild the setup. Keep both.
fieldGuide.output.0.title: Compose the frame
fieldGuide.output.0.body: Check the camera, playhead and selected output settings. Important action should remain readable at the final crop, not just in the editing workspace.
fieldGuide.output.1.title: Capture the result
fieldGuide.output.1.body: Use a still for a single moment and video for movement over time. Review the exported file for framing and timing before using it in promotional material.
fieldGuide.output.2.title: Save the recipe
fieldGuide.output.2.body: Export the scene JSON alongside the media. It preserves the setup for another capture or edit; the image alone cannot restore actors, camera keys and event timing.
fieldGuide.recipe.overview: Recreate the setup behind a frame, then adapt it to your own shot.
fieldGuide.recipe.0.title: Copy the scene
fieldGuide.recipe.0.body: Copy the recipe with the button below. The data records scene settings such as map, actors, camera and timeline; a preview image only shows the intended result.
fieldGuide.recipe.1.title: Load in Studio
fieldGuide.recipe.1.body: Open Scene Studio and use its JSON load controls to restore the recipe. Loading a recipe changes the current scene, so save work you want to keep first.
fieldGuide.recipe.2.title: Review and adapt
fieldGuide.recipe.2.body: Check the camera and playhead after loading, then adjust the shot and capture again. Recipes preserve scene intent; later renderer or asset changes can alter the resulting pixels.

docs.guide.simulation.6.p1: Movement runs at a fixed sixty steps per second. Engine power, weight, forward and reverse limits, track condition, terrain resistance and hull rotation jointly determine handling. The renderer interpolates those states rather than changing movement with frame rate. Handbrake behavior is grounded; landing after a jump must not silently latch the brake.
docs.guide.simulation.6.p2: A fall is a physical impact, not just a height threshold. Mass, impact speed, attitude and mode physics affect the result. Reduced gravity changes both your arc and the terrain you can safely reach. Avoid blind drops at bridge abutments or cliff edges; use a route with a visible landing and enough room to settle.
docs.guide.ai.1.p1: Classic and Jev share the local driving, aiming, visibility and vehicle-system logic on both allied and enemy teams. Jev adds bounded team-level orders; it does not bypass spotting or replace the physical driver. Choose the brain and difficulty before the next match. An allied team should not retain an older behavior set just because it fights alongside the player.
docs.guide.ai.1.p2: Flag teams distribute recovery, escort and raiding roles. Turbo Ball retains a striker long enough to circle behind the ball and line up a push, with screening and defensive support. Zone teams distribute capture pressure. Mobile units can flank while anchors maintain pressure; navigation includes right-of-way for the human, committed passing and safe reversing when vehicles block one another.
docs.guide.ai.2.t: Smoke, remote guns and safe jumps
docs.guide.ai.2.p1: Bots can deploy fitted smoke when withdrawing, under pressure or reloading, and operate remote automatic guns against eligible visible opponents. They only request a jump when the mode allows it and the prospective landing is affordable. Cliff and bridge approaches need a valid route; a direct line to the objective is not enough.
docs.guide.ai.2.p2: Behavior tests include all 33 maps, flag and ball scenarios, congestion, fall-risk decisions and a large Jev team workload. Their guarantees are scoped to the tested scenarios: they catch regressions in decisions and bounded work, but do not prove that a bot will solve every possible terrain or traffic situation.
docs.guide.rendering.1.p1: Driving lights use actual model apertures and follow the hull’s pose. Their warm beams now illuminate farther ahead; only the nearest eligible sources occupy a fixed light pool, while the other visible lamp lenses may still glow. Switching lights off or destroying a tank removes its contribution. Periscopes, mirrors and unrelated armor must not glow just because they share a material.
docs.guide.rendering.1.p2: Ambient occlusion and cast shadows are separate. Turning AO off should not remove sun shadows. Shadow stability, cloud history and effects composition have dedicated checks for moving cameras, firing and quality changes. Smoke is both a rendered volume effect and a simulation visibility blocker; the picture and the spotting decision have separate owners that must agree.
docs.guide.performance.1.p1: The browser may reclaim a graphics context under memory pressure. The game pauses presentation and restores resources behind cover before resuming. Quality recovery should be bounded, preserve the battle state and avoid repeated allocation. A reload is the fallback when restoration cannot complete; it is not the normal way to switch maps or vehicles.
docs.guide.performance.1.p2: When a regular tab behaves differently from a fresh tab, compare the served application version and saved graphics settings before attributing it to one render effect. Hashed assets and deployment-version checks protect against mixed releases. Record the map, vehicle, quality, viewport and reproduction steps with a report; a screenshot alone cannot establish whether the cause is stale assets, settings or GPU state.

fieldGuide.smoke.overview: Smoke is an active spotting countermeasure. This sequence uses the real Abrams launcher sockets, ballistic trajectories and game smoke effect.
fieldGuide.smoke.0.title: Launch ahead of the turret
fieldGuide.smoke.0.label: Ballistic arcs
fieldGuide.smoke.0.body: Press the Smoke control (G by default). Canisters leave the actual launcher banks and fly forward in arcs matching their directions. The two dashed trajectories come from this launch’s simulation. Terrain determines where each canister lands.
fieldGuide.smoke.1.title: Put the screen between you
fieldGuide.smoke.1.label: Sightline screen
fieldGuide.smoke.1.body: After landing, the clouds grow, drift and fade. A sufficiently dense screen across a sightline obstructs spotting and can deny bots a clear engagement. Smoke does not absorb shells: use the cover to reposition rather than staying where the enemy last saw you.
fieldGuide.smoke.2.title: Budget your salvos
fieldGuide.smoke.2.label: Charges & cooldown
fieldGuide.smoke.2.body: An equipped vehicle starts with 3 salvos. Each launch spends one and starts a 28-second cooldown. The effect expires 18 seconds after launch; travel and growth use part of that time. Watch the live counter and timer before relying on another screen.

studio.director.ui.preset.golden-advance: Two Leopards cross the farm fields in low gold light: a head-on portrait, a track-level pass, a reveal over the barns.
A column grinds up the snow road at first light: a rear follow, a close look at the running gear, a high reveal.
studio.director.ui.preset.fields-assault: Four tanks advance under their own barrage: a column from behind, the second gun firing, the line opening up from above.
studio.director.ui.preset.night-knockout: Under a parachute flare a T-90 meets a Leopard at the church crossroads: the approach, the exchange, the kill.
Two heavies roll under the ironworks gantries by flarelight, guns trained down the yard.
studio.director.ui.preset.railyard-salvo: Three Abrams fire down the rails at golden hour while the far yard takes a barrage.
A Swedish pair meets a T-80 across the alpine lake: rear follow, the first round, the kill from above.
studio.director.ui.preset.dawn-patrol.de: Japanese armor moves out of the frontier farms at dawn: the tracks close up, a low pass, the basin from above.
studio.director.ui.preset.fjord-road.des: Challengers follow the shore road through the fjord village, the water beside them all the way.
A British column leaves the harbor as the light goes gold: head-on, from behind, then the whole bay.
studio.director.ui.preset.oasis-sunset.d: Merkavas cross the oasis as the sun sets behind the palms.
studio.director.ui.preset.orchard-column: Three Italian vehicles thread the orchard rows: from above, at track level, then the valley.
Chinese armor follows the delta road through a waking river village.
studio.director.ui.preset.temple-road.de: A lone K2 climbs the monsoon road past the temple: its tracks, a low pass, the ridge from above.
studio.director.ui.preset.reservoir-dusk: Chieftains skirt the reservoir after sunset, the lake still holding the light.
studio.director.ui.preset.walking-barrag: A night assault behind a walking barrage, lit by a flare: the guns, the column, the fire ahead.
studio.director.ui.preset.alpine-village: A Leopard and a CV90 roll through the mountain village under the peaks.
A KF51 at full speed across the frontier at sunset: the gun from the front, the tracks, the dust trail from above.
